name: Marketing agency hero: large centered headline permanently clipped to an inverted-color window of a city-lights photo, shifting as the page scrolls
notes: Every line of the headline is masked now — no plain fallback line. Each h1 span sets background-image to the same hero photo, background-clip:text, then filter:invert(1) saturate(1.3) contrast(1.3) brightness(1.2), so the letters read as a bright inverted-color 'window' cut into the dark photo behind them, permanently on. Runs on city-lights-night.jpg (a starry night skyline with saturated red/teal/blue reflections) because the color variety and inverted starfield read as literal texture through the letters; pick a similarly high-contrast, colorful night/light-source photo if swapping it out, not a flat daylight shot. Both image layers are pinned to the viewport rather than scrolling with the page — .hero-bg is position:fixed and .mask-heading span uses background-attachment:fixed — so as the page scrolls, the pinned crop stays put while the headline (normal in-flow content) slides over it, and each letter reveals a different part of the same image as it moves past. That's the whole point of leaving the invert filter on permanently instead of one plain line: the shifting-through-the-lens effect needs to be visible across the full headline, not just two of three words. Verified via getComputedStyle(...).position/backgroundAttachment staying 'fixed' at scrollY 0, 150, and 500+ on desktop, and the visible crop behind the letters changing as hero-main scrolls up over the still-pinned background. .hero-main is now align-items:center + text-align:center (was left-aligned) and the heading's clamp() runs much larger (up to 11rem) — deliberately large and centered per the brief, not just 'bigger than before'. The old dark linear-gradient shadow over the photo (.hero::after) is gone entirely so the city itself reads bright and clear; non-masked text (eyebrow, dek, ghost button, foot stats) got text-shadow and/or a small blurred dark pill background instead, scoped to just that text, so nothing dims the photo globally. Both fixed layers still fall back to normal scroll under 720px width and prefers-reduced-motion, per the same iOS-jank and vestibular-motion reasoning as before.
